query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by whether the alloy is a single-phase solid solution. A single-phase state—by virtue of high configurational entropy—promotes a homogeneous cation distribution that enables the growth of a slow-growing, chemically inert oxide whose lattice structure is well‐matched to the substrate, reducing interfacial stresses. In multiphase alloys, compositional and structural inhomogeneities create phase boundaries that serve as stress concentrators, leading to increased susceptibility to cracking and spallation of the oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys synthesized as either a single-phase solid solution or a multiphase metallic structure.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy samples to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in a controlled oxidative/corrosive environment with fixed oxygen partial pressure and similar heating/cooling rates for all samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherence between the protective oxide scale and the alloy substrate, mediated by uniform cation distribution in a single-phase alloy (which promotes a close lattice match and low mismatch strain) versus the stress heterogeneities present at phase boundaries in multiphase alloys.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in single-phase alloys ensures a random and homogeneous distribution of metal cations. This uniformity favors the formation of well-adherent, slow-growing oxide scales (for example, protective Al2O3 or SiO2 layers, depending on X) that match the substrate lattice and accommodate thermal expansion. In multiphase alloys, instead, compositional segregation at phase boundaries leads to localized variations in oxide scale formation kinetics and different thermal expansion coefficients, promoting the build-up of interfacial stresses that result in cracking and spallation of the oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature oxidative/corrosive conditions, single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys will develop and maintain a coherent and slow-growing oxide layer, while multiphase samples will more frequently exhibit oxide cracking and spallation.
generation.baseline: A defined comparison against alloys with either no additional reactive element (i.e., CrFeCoNi without X) or against the same CrFeCoNiX composition processed to yield a multiphase structure, under identical exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The test applies to exposures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, with alloy compositions restricted to CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) and evaluating performance over extended exposure durations relevant to high-temperature applications.
generation.uncertainty: The specific role and oxide chemistry of each additional element (Si, Mn, or Al) in determining the oxide phase formation and stability remain not fully quantified and may show variation with atmospheric conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX alloy samples (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) in both single-phase solid solution and multiphase states. Expose the samples in a controlled furnace at temperatures above 900 °C under an oxidative/corrosive atmosphere for a set period. Use in-situ high-temperature microscopy (or periodic ex-situ SEM/TEM analysis) to monitor the evolution of the oxide layer over time, including its morphology, thickness, and adherence.
measurements: Oxide layer continuity and morphology via SEM/TEM imaging
Crack density and spallation area assessments
Weight gain measurements as an indirect measure of oxidation kinetics
Adhesion tests of the oxide scale (e.g., through scratch tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under identical exposure conditions, the single-phase alloys show rates of oxide cracking or spallation that are statistically indistinguishable from those observed in multiphase samples, then the hypothesis that phase homogeneity (via high configurational entropy) governs the superior stability of the protective oxide layer would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Entropy-stabilized oxides

Abstract: Configurational disorder can be compositionally engineered into mixed oxide by populating a single sublattice with many distinct cations. The formulations promote novel and entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter where metal cations are incorporated in new ways. Here, through rigorous experiments, a simple thermodynamic model, and a five-component oxide formulation, we demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state. In the latter, cation distributions are proven to be random and homogeneous. The findings validate the hypothesis that deliberate configurational disorder provides an orthogonal strategy to imagine and discover new phases of crystalline matter and untapped opportunities for property engineering. The composition of oxide compounds controls many of their properties and electronic phases. Here, the authors show that entropy and configurational disorder can stabilize new phases of oxides, potentially enabling a better engineering of their properties.
